significance: The Bamberg mass prosecution (1626–1631) was the most intensive witch hunt in the Holy Roman Empire outside Trier, resulting in approximately 300–400 executions from 900+ accusations in five years. It began when a hailstorm was blamed on witches and court midwife Margaretha Binder was arrested; the cascade mechanism then spread through all social strata including court officials, clergy, and ultimately the mayor himself. The trials ended only with Prince-Bishop Fuchs von Dornheim's death in 1631. Friedrich Spee's Cautio criminalis (1631) is widely understood as a response to the conditions that produced Bamberg and Würzburg.
source_method: Trial records in Bamberg episcopal archives; analysis in Behringer, Witchcraft Persecutions in Bavaria (1997); Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (2016)
